it.

## Lecture Plan

- **Measurement Error.** Noise in a regressor pulls its coefficient toward zero.
- **Reverse Causality.** Regression is symmetric. Causation is not.
- **The Road to Part II.** One design at a time, named by the problem it solves.

::: {.tablenotes}
Reading: [to settle].

## The Data-Generating Process Behind the Sample

**The objective of these four lines:** show what has actually been producing
the hundred and twenty rows you have worked with all term.

```{=latex}
\begin{align*}
A_i     &= \text{ability, drawn once and never recorded} \\
S_i     &= 13.5 + \gamma A_i + u_i \\
Y_i     &= 9.50 + 1.30\,(S_i - 12) + \delta A_i + \varepsilon_i \\
S^{*}_i &= S_i + m_i
\end{align*}
```

and a person appears in your data only if $Y_i \ge f$.

- $A_i$: ability, which nobody measured
- $\gamma$: how much ability raises schooling
- $\delta$: how much ability raises pay
- $S^{*}_i$: the schooling the person reported
- $m_i$: the reporting error
- $f$: the wage floor

## Why These Faults Leave No Trace in the Residuals

- **4.1** was heteroskedasticity, serial correlation, the wrong shape. Each
  one leaves a signature in the residuals, and each one has a response.
- **4.2** is ability, mismeasurement and selection. Each one leaves the
  residual plot looking exactly as it should.

::: {.takeaway title="The point of the whole session"}
There is no diagnostic for today's faults, because a correctly specified
regression of the wrong thing on the wrong thing fits beautifully. You cannot
test your way out of this. You design your way out, and that is what Part II
is for.
:::

# Measurement Error

## What the Regression Recovers When Schooling Is Mismeasured

**The goal of this section:** say what noise in a regressor does to its own
coefficient, and why it does the opposite of what noise sounds like it should.

**The objective of this expression:** say what the regression recovers when
the $x$ you have is the $x$ you want plus noise.

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\beta_1 \times \frac{\sigma_S^2}{\sigma_S^2 + \sigma_m^2}
\end{equation}
```

- $\sigma_S^2$: the variance of actual schooling
- $\sigma_m^2$: the variance of the reporting error

<!-- IDEA 1. 18-38 min. The fraction has a name, the reliability ratio,
     and it is worth saying out loud that it is a proportion of variance
     that is signal. -->

## Why the Reliability Ratio Shrinks the Estimate

::: {.result}
The fraction sits between zero and one. So the estimate is smaller than the
truth in absolute value, and it is smaller every single time rather than on
average. Noisier reporting, smaller coefficient. This is attenuation.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
At zero error the fraction is one and the estimate is the truth. If the
reporting error had the same variance as schooling itself, you would recover
half the return and your standard error would tell you nothing was wrong.
:::

## How the Estimate Falls as Reporting Error Grows

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The estimated return against the standard
deviation of the reporting error. The dashed green line is the truth. The
estimate decays toward zero and never crosses it.}
```

<!-- FIGURE 4-2_attenuation: sweep B_04_03 misreport_sd from 0 to about
     3.5 years, draw the population once per value, fit, and plot the
     slope. Green dashed reference at B_03_02_true_slope_dbl. One extra
     series in light blue: the estimate from the same draws using
     actual_yrs, which stays flat on the truth. -->

## Where the Noise Lands in the Slope Formula

The closed form you derived for homework in week 4 is a covariance over a
variance. Adding independent noise to schooling leaves the covariance with
earnings alone, because the noise has nothing to do with earnings. It adds to
the variance underneath.

::: {.caveat title="This is the counter-intuitive bit"}
Noise in a regressor does two things, not one. It widens the sampling
distribution, which you expected. It also drags the centre of that
distribution toward zero, which you did not, and the drag is in the same
direction every time.
:::

## Three Cases Where Attenuation Does Not Apply

- **Noise in $y$** does not bias the slope at all. It inflates the standard
  error and leaves the coefficient where it was.
- **Noise in a control** in a multiple regression can push the coefficient you
  care about in either direction.
- **Non-classical error** breaks the result outright: people who round their
  schooling up are not a random selection @bound2001.

::: {.tablenotes}
The classical case is the one with a clean answer, and the literature on the
return to schooling has argued about exactly this since @griliches1977. It is
also why the twin studies are awkward: differencing two siblings removes the
family, but it removes far more real schooling than reporting error, so the
differenced estimate is the more attenuated one @ashenfelter1994.
:::

## Vote: Which Survey Gives the Smaller Estimate?

Two surveys measure the same return. In one, people report their own years of
schooling. In the other, the years come from the school register.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue with your neighbour, vote again. Then: is the difference between
them a matter of luck, or would it come out the same way again?
:::

# Reverse Causality

## The Same Data Fitted in Both Directions

**The goal of this section:** show that the regression is symmetric in its two
variables, that causation is not, and that the output cannot tell them apart.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The same hundred and twenty people, with
earnings on schooling in navy and schooling on earnings in green. Both are
least squares. Both are correct. They are different lines.}
```

<!-- IDEA 2. 40-62 min. No switch needed - this is C_02_05_sample_df with
     the axes swapped and the second fit drawn back on the original axes. -->

<!-- FIGURE 4-2_reversed: scatter of the working sample, the y-on-x fit,
     and the x-on-y fit inverted onto the same axes. Subtitle carries both
     implied returns so the room sees two numbers, not two lines. -->

## The Algebra Behind the Two Fitted Slopes

**The objective of these two expressions:** show that the difference between
the two fits is arithmetic rather than rhetorical.

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\hat{\beta}_{Y \mid S} = \frac{s_{SY}}{s_S^2}
\qquad\qquad
\hat{\beta}_{S \mid Y} = \frac{s_{SY}}{s_Y^2}
\end{equation}
```

- $\hat{\beta}_{Y \mid S}$: the slope from regressing earnings on schooling
- $\hat{\beta}_{S \mid Y}$: the slope from regressing schooling on earnings
- $s_{SY}$: the sample covariance of schooling and earnings
- $s_S^2$: the sample variance of schooling
- $s_Y^2$: the sample variance of earnings

::: {.result}
The numerator is the same in both. The two slopes differ only in which
variance sits underneath, and their product is the R-squared you learned to
read in week 5.
:::

## Simultaneity: When Causation Runs in Both Directions

Sometimes the honest picture is not one direction or the other but both.
Price and quantity are settled together, so a regression of quantity on price
traces out neither the demand curve nor the supply curve @working1927. Naming
that problem is what founded the subject @haavelmo1943.

::: {.caveat title="And in our own example"}
If you stay in school longer because you expect to earn more, then earnings
expectations cause schooling at the same time as schooling causes earnings.
Both arrows are live, and the slope is a blend of the two.
:::

## The Regression Output Is Identical Either Way

- The R-squared is identical whichever variable you called $y$.
- The t-statistic is identical.
- The residual plot is clean in both directions.
- A larger sample makes both answers more precise and neither more correct.

::: {.takeaway}
Direction is not in the data. It comes from timing, from institutions, from
what could not possibly have caused what - and, in Part II, from a design
built to make one direction the only one available.
:::

# The Road to Part II

## Instrumental Variables, for a Confounder Nobody Measured

**The goal of this section:** name each remaining problem and the design that
exists to answer it. One idea each, and no technique.

::: {.defn title="The idea"}
Find something that moves schooling and has no other route to earnings. Use
only the part of schooling that it moves, and throw the rest away.
:::

Compulsory-schooling laws move how long some people stay in school without
having anything else to do with their wages @angrist1991. The schooling
literature is largely a long argument about which of these candidates
survives scrutiny @card1999.

<!-- IDEA 3. 64-88 min. One frame per design. Name the problem, state the
     idea in a sentence, give one real study. No estimator, no algebra,
     no two-stage anything - that is Part II's first month. -->

## Difference-in-Differences and Fixed Effects, for What Is Constant

::: {.defn title="The idea"}
If the thing you cannot see does not change, compare a unit with itself over
time, or compare the change in a treated group against the change in an
untreated one. Whatever is constant subtracts out.
:::

Employment in fast-food restaurants either side of a state border, before and
after one state raised its minimum wage @cardkrueger1994. Or two siblings with
the same parents and different schooling @ashenfelter1994.

::: {.tablenotes}
What is differenced away never has to be measured. That is the whole trick,
and it is also the whole limitation: anything that changes is still there.
:::

## Regression Discontinuity, for a Rule That Assigns Treatment

::: {.defn title="The idea"}
When a published threshold decides who is treated, the people just above and
just below it are otherwise alike. The jump at the cutoff is the effect.
:::

The design was invented to evaluate scholarship awards handed out on a test
score @thistlethwaite1960, and economics found it again in a class-size rule
that splits a year group once it passes forty pupils @angrist1999. The survey
to start from is @lee2010.

## What the Three Designs Share and What They Cost

- Each one buys a comparison you can defend out loud.
- Each one pays for it with a narrower question and fewer people it applies to.
- None of them is a better estimator. Least squares is usually still what runs.

::: {.takeaway}
The change is in where the credibility comes from. It stops coming from the
model and starts coming from how the data were generated. That argument was
made against the regressions of the day by @leamer1983con, taken up as a
programme by @angrist2010, and given a Nobel lecture by @card2022.
:::

## Why These Designs Are Left Until Part II

@angrist2017undergraduate argue that a first course built on assumptions and
corrections leaves students unable to read a modern applied paper, and the
survey evidence is that most first courses still look much like that
@harter2022. Against them: @sims2010, that an approach which answers only the
questions an experiment can reach leaves most of economics unanswered;
@keane2010, that a design rests on assumptions too, only unstated ones; and
@deaton2010, that an estimate you can defend here is not one you can carry
elsewhere.

::: {.caveat title="Where this module stands"}
You cannot judge an instrument without knowing what a standard error is, and
you cannot see why a design is needed until you have watched a regression
fail. Part I was that, deliberately. Part II is where the designs are taught.
:::

## Vote: Which Design Would You Reach For?

A maintenance grant is paid to every student whose Leaving Certificate points

::: {.tablenotes}

would have to be true about students either side of the cut-off?

## What Would Have To Be True?

::: {.caveat title="The standing question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

[Candidate this week: one published estimate, circulated in advance. Groups of
four, seven minutes, four questions.]

1. What is the number, in its units, and what does the sentence around it claim?
2. What would have to be true of the population for that sentence to be right?
3. Which of this term's faults is the most plausible story where it isn't?
4. What design would answer it, and what would that design cost you?

## What Regression Cannot Do

Today was three separate ideas, each doing one job:

::: {.contributions}
1. **Measurement Error.** Noise in a regressor pulls its coefficient toward zero, and it does so every time rather than on average.
2. **Reverse Causality.** Regression is symmetric and causation is not, and no line of the output records which direction you meant.
3. **The Road to Part II.** Each design exists because one of these faults cannot be diagnosed, only designed around.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Part II begins where this stopped: not with a better estimator, but with a
better reason to believe the comparison.
:::

## Derivation: Attenuation From Classical Measurement Error

Write the slope as a covariance over a variance, substitute reported
schooling for actual schooling, and see which of the two pieces the noise
touches.

::: {.tablenotes}
Three steps. Substitute $S^{*} = S + m$ into the numerator and use the
assumption that $m$ is independent of everything else, so the numerator does
not change. Substitute it into the denominator, where the variances add.
Divide. The step that does the work is the second, and the whole result is
that the noise lands underneath and not on top.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]
